Full
fo͝ol
adj. (filled, containing all it can hold; rendering Hebrew male, Greek pleres, with the noun pleroma, fulness)
From Saxon ful, akin to Latin plenus. Scripture's decisive uses are not about quantity but about what fills — grace and truth, the Holy Ghost, the Godhead bodily.

Biblical Definition

Full in Scripture is almost always answered by the question full of what, and the answers are the doctrine. John says of the incarnate Word that He “dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). Both together, and neither diluted by the other — a fulness of grace that does not soften truth, a fulness of truth that does not withhold grace. Paul presses further and states the deity without remainder: “For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Colossians 2:9). All the fulness, and bodily; the verse is the standing refutation of every scheme that makes Christ a partial vessel of deity or a temporary one. From the Head the word descends to the members. The qualification the apostles required for the first deacons was not administrative: “look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom” (Acts 6:3) — the plainest table service in the church demanded men who were full. And our Lord makes fulness a matter of the eye and therefore of the whole man: “if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light” (Matthew 6:22). Fulness, in every case, is received rather than generated; a vessel does not fill itself, and the whole biblical usage assumes a giver standing outside the container.

Webster 1828 Definition

Replete; having within all that the space will contain. Scripture's weight falls on the contents — full of grace and truth, full of the Holy Ghost, and in Christ all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.

expand to see more

FULL, a. [Sax. ful; L. plenus.] Replete; having within its limits all that it can contain; as a vessel full of water.

2. Abounding with; having a large supply or abundance; as a house full of furniture; a land full of corn.

3. Complete; entire; not defective or partial; as a full account; the full assurance of faith.

4. Saturated; having the mind or heart occupied; as full of thought; full of grace and truth. John 1.

5. Adequate; sufficient; as full satisfaction. Fulness, n. the state of being filled; completeness. In him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. Col. 2.

Key Scripture

John 1:14 — "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth."

Colossians 2:9 — "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily."

Acts 6:3 — "Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business."

Matthew 6:22 — "The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light."

Modern Corruption

Fulness has been turned inward and renamed fulfilment — a life that feels complete — so that the biblical question full of what is answered with myself, and the vessel is asked to supply its own contents.

expand to see more

The promise of a full life is everywhere, and it is almost always a promise about the self: potential realized, purpose discovered, the authentic person finally at home in his own skin. Scripture uses the same adjective and never once locates the contents inside the container. Men are full of the Holy Ghost, full of faith and power, full of goodness and knowledge; the Word made flesh is full of grace and truth; the Godhead dwells in Christ bodily. In every case something has come in from outside. This is not a quibble about phrasing — it decides what a man does when he feels empty. Told that fulness is latent within, he will search himself, and find that the search itself is the emptiness. Told that fulness is given, he will ask, and Christ's standing offer is to the thirsty rather than to the resourceful.

The second distortion is quantitative — the idea that fulness is a matter of more, and that the Christian life is measured in volume of activity. Acts 6:3 corrects it in an unexpected place. The office being filled is the distribution of food to widows, and the requirement is men full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom. The apostles did not scale the qualification to the visibility of the task. And Matthew 6:22 explains the mechanism: fulness of light in the whole body follows from a single eye — an undivided aim. So the road to fulness is not accumulation but singleness, which is why the divided man is always the empty one, and why the remedy Scripture prescribes for emptiness is repentance rather than enrichment.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew male (to fill, be full); Greek pleres (full), pleroo (to fill, fulfil), and pleroma (fulness, that which fills) — the noun Paul uses of the Godhead in Christ and of the church as His body.

expand to see more

Hebrew male (H4390) — to fill, be full, accomplish; used of the glory filling the tabernacle and of days being fulfilled.

Greek pleres (G4134) — full, complete; the word in “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14) and “full of the Holy Ghost” (Acts 6:3).

Greek pleroma (G4138) — fulness, that which fills; used of the Godhead dwelling bodily in Christ (Colossians 2:9).

Greek pleroo (G4137) — to fill, complete, fulfil; the verb behind being filled with the Spirit and with the knowledge of His will.

Greek haplous (G573) — single, simple, without fold; the eye of Matthew 6:22 whose singleness fills the body with light.

Usage

"“Full of grace and truth” — both at once, neither diluting the other."

"“All the fulness of the Godhead bodily” — deity without remainder, in a body."

"“Full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom” — the qualification for waiting on tables."
